passage: Nitin dropped his bag by the door of the fourth-floor flat and did not take his shoes off. "Do you even care that I have a match on Saturday?" he said to his mother, Hafsa, who was stirring dal and had just asked him to fold the laundry first. Hafsa heard the edge in his voice. She could have listed everything she had done for him that month. Instead she turned the gas low. "You sound like today was heavy. Is it the match, or something else?" Nitin shrugged and kicked off one shoe. "Coach might bench me." After a pause he added, "Leave the laundry, I'll do it." Hafsa sat beside him, still unsure whether the sharp question had been hurt, anger or just a way to start talking.

qa.q: Where did Nitin drop his bag?
qa.a: He dropped it by the door of the fourth-floor flat.

qa.q: What might Nitin have been feeling when he asked whether his mother even cares?
qa.a: Most likely hurt and worried about being benched, since he later mentions the coach might bench him. It could also have been plain anger at being asked to do laundry first.

qa.q: What could Hafsa try next if Nitin goes quiet again?
qa.a: She could keep answering the feeling underneath, for example by saying he seems upset and asking what happened, rather than defending herself against the words.

qa.q: How might Hafsa have felt when Nitin asked if she even cared?
qa.a: Hafsa may have felt stung and tempted to list everything she had done, but she chose to stay calm and ask what was heavy. Even afterwards she was still unsure what lay behind the question.

grounding: A teen's rhetorical question read as hurt, anger or sarcasm, and the parent answers the feeling rather than the words.

"Wow, thanks for the ride to school, really. Best sister ever."
"Trisha, that's sarcasm, isn't it?"
"No, it's a compliment." She stared at the window.
"You didn't even remember the recital rehearsal yesterday, did you?" Trisha said. "Do you ever look at anything except your phone?"
"I was stuck at college till late," said Deepika. "But you're upset I missed it. Am I right?"
Trisha picked at her bag strap. "Maybe."
"Then tell me that instead of asking if I care. I do care. Show me the song after dinner?"
"Fine." Trisha's mouth twitched. "But you have to sit through it twice."

qa.q: What did Trisha say to Deepika at the start of the ride?
qa.a: She said, "Wow, thanks for the ride to school, really. Best sister ever."

qa.q: Why does Trisha pick at her bag strap when Deepika says she is upset?
qa.a: It suggests she feels caught and a little vulnerable, since her sarcasm covered real disappointment about the missed rehearsal. It might also just be restlessness.

qa.q: What did Deepika do that worked?
qa.a: She named the feeling behind the sarcasm, admitted she missed the rehearsal, and offered a concrete way to make it up.

qa.q: What might Deepika's honesty change for Trisha?
qa.a: Trisha may feel safe to say she was hurt directly next time, instead of hiding it in a sharp question.

grounding: A teen's sarcastic and rhetorical remarks carry hurt, and a sibling answers the feeling behind them.

passage:
Last winter I came home from a terrible football trial and found Trisha didi on the sofa, laughing into her phone. I dropped my boots by the door and said, loudly, "Does anyone in this house even care what happens to me?"
Didi could have said, "Obviously, Yogesh, don't be dramatic." That is what I expected, and honestly what I was ready to fight.
Instead she put the phone face down. "Bad trial?"
I said, "Whatever." Then I sat on the arm of the sofa, which is what I do when I want someone to keep asking.
"Coach picked the others?" she asked.
I nodded, and the whole story came out: the missed pass, the boys smirking.
Looking back, my question wasn't really a question. It was the trial talking. She answered that part, and the fight never started.

qa.q: Where was Trisha when Yogesh came home from the trial?
qa.a: Trisha didi was on the sofa, laughing into her phone.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when asking if anyone even cared, and what else might the question have meant?
qa.a: Yogesh was most likely hurt and embarrassed after the bad trial, and the loud question was that disappointment spilling over. It could also have carried some anger at seeing his sister laughing while he felt low.

qa.q: Which choice of Trisha's worked, and why?
qa.a: Putting the phone down and asking "Bad trial?" worked, because it answered the feeling under the question instead of arguing with its words, so Yogesh felt safe enough to tell the story.

qa.q: How might Trisha have seen the question if she had taken it literally?
qa.a: She might have felt accused of not caring and snapped back, and then the two of them would have been arguing about her phone instead of talking about the trial.

grounding: The account shows a teenager's rhetorical question carrying hurt, and a sister responding to the feeling rather than the literal words.

passage:
Class 9B, Thursday, second period.
When I set the group project on water use, Karthik leaned back and said, "Why do we even do these? Does anyone actually read them?" Two boys laughed. His tone was sharp, and my first urge was to explain the marking scheme.
I noticed a few things instead. Karthik's folder had last term's project in it, still with no comments on it; I had returned it late and unmarked because of the exams. He was not looking at me while he spoke, but at the folder.
So I did not defend the project. After class I asked him, "Did it feel like nobody read your last one?" He shrugged and said, "Kind of. I worked on it for a month."
I apologised, gave him written feedback on it by Friday, and he chose the hardest topic this time.
Minakshi Rao, class teacher

qa.q: What did Karthik have in his folder?
qa.a: Karthik's folder had last term's project in it, still with no comments on it.

qa.q: What does Karthik's gaze at the folder suggest about his mood behind the sarcastic question?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and let down that his month of work seemed unread, not just bored or rude. His sarcasm could also have been partly showing off for the boys who laughed.

qa.q: What could a teacher learn from how Minakshi handled the remark?
qa.a: Instead of defending the task in front of the class, a teacher could ask privately about the feeling behind a sarcastic question and fix any real cause, as Minakshi did with the late feedback.

qa.q: If you were one of the boys who laughed, how might you have read Karthik's question?
qa.a: You might have heard it as a funny, cheeky jab at homework, with no idea that it came from a project he cared about and felt ignored on.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a sarcastic rhetorical question hiding hurt, and an adult answering the feeling rather than the literal complaint.

passage:
Sunday night
Dolma texted at 7: "wow ok. do you even care about our plan or no?"
My first reply was all facts. I had gone to Nani's because Mummy asked, I had told Dolma on Friday (sort of), and the art-fair plan could move to next week. Sent. Felt clever.
She wrote back one word: "sure."
That "sure" sat in my chest for an hour. Dolma doesn't do one-word replies. So I stopped defending and called her.
"You sound upset," I said. "Is it the fair, or something else?"
Long pause. Then it came out: she'd been waiting at the bus stop for forty minutes, and the others had gone without her too. She felt like the spare friend.
I said sorry for real this time, not with reasons. We're going next Saturday, just us two.
- Devika

qa.q: How long had Dolma waited at the bus stop?
qa.a: Dolma had been waiting at the bus stop for forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Dolma most likely feeling behind her question, and what is another possible reading?
qa.a: Dolma most likely felt hurt and left out, like "the spare friend" after waiting alone. Another reading is that she was simply angry at being let down about the art fair.

qa.q: What went wrong with Devika's first reply, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Devika answered the literal question with facts and excuses, which made Dolma go cold. Calling and asking about the feeling, then apologising without reasons, fixed it.

qa.q: What was it like for Dolma to get a list of reasons after waiting forty minutes?
qa.a: It probably felt like being argued with instead of heard, which is why she replied with a flat "sure" and pulled back.

grounding: The diary shows a friend's rhetorical text carrying hurt, and the writer learning to answer the feeling rather than the literal words.

qa.q: What time did Swati say it was?
qa.a: Swati said it was 7:15, though the plan was 6.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling behind the question 'do you even care'?
qa.a: Swati was most likely hurt and angry after looking at the back row through the whole solo. The sarcastic 'great excuse' may hide disappointment more than a real doubt that Hrithik cares.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik's reply work better than arguing?
qa.a: Hrithik answered the feeling, naming the hurt and the missed solo, instead of debating the literal question, and then offered a concrete way to make up for it.

qa.q: What would change if Hrithik had simply replied 'Of course I care'?
qa.a: It would answer the words but not the hurt, so Swati would likely feel brushed off and push back harder.

grounding: It shows a rhetorical 'do you even care' carrying hurt and sarcasm, and a reply that answers the feeling behind it rather than the literal words.
